summary: Defines how ForCES messages are carried over SCTP, the Transport Mapping Layer for ForCES. It explains why SCTP was chosen and how it meets the requirements. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: ForCES lets the software that controls a router run somewhere other than the router itself, so the control element and the forwarding element need a way to talk. This document defines that link over SCTP, the transport protocol. It opens three separate SCTP connections between the two, so that urgent configuration work is not stuck behind a flood of less important messages.

subtitle: How ForCES control and forwarding elements talk over SCTP, using three prioritized channels.

tldr.problem: The ForCES protocol layer needs a transport underneath that offers reliability, congestion control, prioritization, high availability and security between control elements and forwarding elements.
tldr.mechanism: The SCTP TML opens three SCTP sockets per CE-FE pair, on ports 6704, 6705 and 6706, for high-priority reliable, medium-priority semi-reliable and low-priority unreliable traffic, and serves them with strict priority scheduling. IPsec provides security.
tldr.outcome: A single transport covers every TML requirement of RFC 5810, and tying node overload to transport congestion keeps important work moving under load.

today: RFC 5811 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2010, and its unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the SCTP mapping for the ForCES protocol of RFC 5810.

sections.title: What ForCES Needs From a Transport
sections.content:
The ForCES working group in the IETF defines the architecture and the protocol for separating control elements and forwarding elements inside network elements such as routers. RFC 3654 and RFC 3746 set out the architectural and protocol requirements for the communication between them, and the ForCES protocol layer specification RFC 5810 describes the protocol semantics and workings.

The ForCES protocol layer operates on top of an interconnect hiding layer known as the Transport Mapping Layer, or TML. This document defines the SCTP-based TML for the ForCES protocol layer, and explains the rationale for choosing SCTP and how the TML addresses the requirements set for it, including security and reliability.

The TML is the layer that hides the transport media from the protocol. It is defined as the layer in the ForCES protocol architecture that specifically addresses protocol message transportation issues, such as how the protocol messages are mapped to different transport media like SCTP, IP, TCP, UDP, ATM or Ethernet, and how reliability and security are achieved.
sections.plainLanguage: ForCES moves the control function of a router out of the router. The control element configures the forwarding element, which does the packet forwarding. This document defines the link between the two, and the transport it uses.

sections.title: The Protocol Layer and the Transport Layer
sections.content:
The ForCES protocol layering has two pieces, the protocol layer and the transport mapping layer. On the control element side there is a CE protocol layer above a CE transport mapping layer; on the forwarding element side there is an FE transport mapping layer above an FE protocol layer, and the ForCES protocol messages travel between the two protocol layers.

The protocol layer is in charge of the ForCES protocol; its semantics and message layout are defined in RFC 5810. It is responsible for associating a forwarding element or a control element with a network element, and for tearing down those associations. The transport mapping layer is necessary to connect two ForCES endpoints. Both layers are standardized by the IETF: only one protocol layer is defined, while different transport mapping layers are expected to be standardized, and the layer at each of the nodes is expected to be of the same definition so that the two ends interoperate.

When transmitting, the protocol layer delivers its messages to the transport mapping layer, which delivers the protocol layer message to the destination transport mapping layer or layers. On reception, the transport mapping layer delivers the message to its destination protocol layer, as described in the ForCES header.

There are two interfaces. The first is between the protocol layer and the transport mapping layer. The second is the control element manager or forwarding element manager interface, which reaches both the protocol layer and the transport mapping layer, and is responsible for bootstrapping and parameterizing the transport mapping layer. In its most basic form that interface takes the form of a simple static configuration file read on startup in the pre-association phase.

It is expected that a configuration reference point, such as the forwarding element manager or the control element manager, can be used to configure the transport mapping layer. The configured parameters may include the protocol layer ID; the connection type and its associated data, such as SCTP ports and IP addresses when the layer uses IP and SCTP; the number of transport connections; the connection capability, such as bandwidth; and the allowed or supported connection quality of service policy, or congestion control policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol layer knows what the messages mean; the transport layer knows how to move them. A configuration file read at startup tells the transport layer the addresses, ports and connection settings it needs, and the two halves of the architecture talk to each other through a small API.

sections.title: Why SCTP
sections.content:
SCTP is an end-to-end transport protocol that is equivalent to TCP, UDP or DCCP in many aspects. With a few exceptions it can do most of what UDP, TCP or DCCP can achieve, and it can do most of what a combination of those protocols can achieve, such as TCP and DCCP or TCP and UDP.

Like TCP it provides ordered, reliable, connection-oriented, flow-controlled and congestion-controlled data exchange, but unlike TCP it does not provide byte streaming and instead provides message boundaries. Like UDP it can provide unreliable, unordered data exchange, but unlike UDP it does not provide multicast support. Like DCCP it can provide unreliable, ordered, congestion-controlled, connection-oriented data exchange.

SCTP also provides services that none of those three transports offer, which the document finds attractive: multi-homing, runtime IP address binding, a range of reliability shades with congestion control, built-in heartbeats, multi-streaming, message boundaries with reliability, improved SYN denial-of-service protection, simpler transport events and simplified replicasting.

The rationale is that SCTP has all the features needed to provide a robust transport mapping layer. As an all-encompassing transport it removes the need for several transport protocols to satisfy the requirements of RFC 5810, which allows simpler coding and therefore reduces interoperability concerns. SCTP is also very mature and widely used, which makes it a good choice for ubiquitous deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: SCTP is a transport like TCP, but it keeps message boundaries instead of turning everything into a byte stream, it can be told to give up on a message after a time limit, and it can use several network addresses at once. That combination meant one transport could do the work of several, which keeps the implementation simpler.

sections.title: The Three Channels
sections.content:
Three channels group and prioritize the work for different types of ForCES traffic, and each channel is an SCTP socket interface with different properties. All SCTP channels are congestion aware. SCTP ports 6704, 6705 and 6706 are used for the higher-, medium- and lower-priority channels, and SCTP Payload Protocol ID values of 21, 22 and 23 identify those channels.

The higher-priority channel uses a standard SCTP reliable socket on port 6704, with PPID 21 for all messages. It carries the messages the control element solicits and their responses: the ForCES configuration messages flowing from the control element to the forwarding element and the responses back, and the ForCES query messages and their responses. PL priorities 4 to 7 MUST be used for all protocol layer messages on this channel. The messages that MUST use it are AssociationSetup, AssociationSetupResponse and AssociationTeardown, each with default priority 7, and Config, ConfigResponse, Query and QueryResponse, each with default priority 4. A response to a ForCES message MUST carry the same priority as the request, so a config sent with priority 5 must have a config response with priority 5. If a message arrives on this channel with a priority outside 4 to 7, the wrong PPID, or a message type other than those listed, the protocol layer message MUST be dropped.

The medium-priority channel uses SCTP-PR, the partial reliability extension, on port 6705, with PPID 22 for all messages. Time limits on how long a message stays valid are set on each outgoing message. It is used for events from the forwarding element to the control element that go stale over time, such as events that are accumulative in nature and that the control element can recover by issuing a query. PL priority 3 MUST be used for messages on this channel, and the Event Notification message, with default priority 3, MUST use it.

The lower-priority channel uses SCTP port 6706, with PPID 23, and it also uses SCTP-PR with lower timeout values than the medium channel. An unreliable channel is used for redirect messages so that the control protocol at both ends can take charge of its own end-to-end semantics: some control protocols are reliable by nature, so adding reliability here would introduce an extra layer that could be harmful and would push retransmissions to the far end, and some want their messages to go stale over time, which reliability would contradict. ForCES protocol layer heartbeats are traffic sensitive, so sending them over this channel also makes sense; if the other end is busy with other channels the heartbeats are obsoleted locally, and it does not matter that they did not arrive. PL priorities 1 to 2 MUST be used on this channel, and the PacketRedirect message, with default priority 2, and the Heartbeat message, with default priority 1, MUST use it.

The document explains why three sockets rather than three streams on one socket. SCTP allows up to 64 K streams over a single socket, and the authors first planned to map each channel to a stream, which would have simplified programming and saved SCTP ports. Further analysis found head-of-line blocking problems with that: lower-priority packets that did not need reliable delivery could block higher-priority packets that did, under congestion, for an indeterminate time depending on how many lower-priority packets were pending. Mapping each channel to a separate socket avoids that.
sections.plainLanguage: Three SCTP connections carry everything. Configuration and query work goes on the reliable one, events that go stale go on the semi-reliable one, and redirected control packets and heartbeats go on the unreliable one. Each connection has its own port and its own protocol identifier, and a message that arrives on the wrong one is dropped.

sections.title: Scheduling the Three Channels
sections.content:
When sending and receiving protocol layer messages, the transport mapping layer core uses strict priority work-conserving scheduling. High priority messages are always processed first until there are none left, and the low priority channel is processed only if the channels with a higher priority have no messages left to process. Under congestion, a higher priority channel with enough messages to occupy the available bandwidth will starve the lower priority channels.

The design intent is to tie processing prioritization and transport congestion control together to provide implicit node congestion control. The work scheduling prioritization scheme is receiver-based processing: fully arrived packets on any of the channels are a source of work whose output may result in transmitted packets, but there is no control over the order in which SCTP, the operating system or the network chooses to send transmitted packets across and make them available to the receiver. The document says it tries to ameliorate this with the choice of channel properties, ForCES message grouping and the tying of control element and forwarding element work scheduling, while admitting that it does not fully resolve the issue.

From a ForCES perspective some reordering can be tolerated. If a forwarding element transmits a configuration response on the high priority channel followed by 10000 OSPF redirect packets on the low priority channel, and the control element gets five OSPF redirects first, that is tolerable. What matters is that the control element gets to the high priority message soon, rather than sitting for long periods processing OSPF packets, which is what would have happened with a single socket carrying three streams.

On overload, when a node's CPU is overwhelmed because the incoming packet rate is higher than it can keep up with, the channel queues grow and transport congestion follows. Because the transport is SCTP, the congestion is propagated back to the source of the incoming packets and eventually alleviated. The high priority channel work is preferred over the medium, which is preferred over the low. The preferential scheduling only kicks in when there is node overload, whether or not there is transport congestion, and as a result the node achieves a robust steady processing capacity.

The example given is a case where a large number of redirected packets coming into the network element may overload the forwarding element while it has outstanding configuration work from the control element. While the forwarding element is busy with configuration requests it essentially ignores the redirect packets on the low priority channel, and if enough of them accumulate they are dropped, either because the low priority channel threshold is exceeded or because they are obsoleted. If the forwarding element has processed the higher priority channels and their work, it can then process the low priority channel. This is how the transport mapping layer ties transport congestion and node overload together.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver always works on the urgent channel first, and only moves to the next when there is nothing urgent left. When a node falls behind, its queues grow and SCTP tells the sender to slow down. Redirected packets pile up and are dropped rather than delaying configuration work.

sections.title: Meeting the Requirements One by One
sections.content:
The document walks through the requirements that a transport mapping layer has to meet and says how the SCTP version meets each one.

Reliability is met because SCTP offers a range of reliability shades. Congestion control is met because it is built into SCTP. Timeliness and prioritization are addressed by using three sockets together with the partial reliability feature. Addressing is met without extra headers, because SCTP can be told to replicast packets to multiple destinations; the transport mapping layer implementation has to translate protocol layer addresses into a variety of unicast IP addresses to emulate multicast and broadcast protocol layer addresses.

High availability is where SCTP is strongest. Failure detection and recovery are built in. The multi-homing feature gives path diversity: if one of the peer IP addresses becomes unreachable, the others are used without lower-layer convergence, or even the transport mapping layer, becoming aware. SCTP heartbeats and data transmission thresholds are used per peer IP address to detect reachability faults, whether caused by an unreachable address or peer because of an interface, network or endpoint failure, and the cause of the fault is noted. With the ADDIP feature, IP addresses can be migrated to other nodes at runtime, much as the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol does, and this is used in addition to multi-homing in a planned migration of activity from one forwarding or control element to another, such as part of the recipe for replacing a forwarding element.

Node overload prevention follows from the three channels and the strict priority scheduling. The fundamental desire of the strict prioritization is to ensure that more important processing work always gets node resources over less important work. When a node's CPU is overwhelmed, the channel queues grow and transport congestion follows, and because the transport is SCTP the congestion is propagated back to the source of the incoming packets. The high priority channel work is prioritized at the expense of the medium, which is prioritized over the low.

Encapsulation is handled by the SCTP payload protocol identifiers, which identify the channels. Parameters needed to boot the transport mapping layer are the IP address or resolvable host name of the peer, whether to use IPsec and how to parameterize the ciphers and keys, and the three SCTP ports, whose defaults are 6704, 6705 and 6706.
sections.plainLanguage: The document checks the SCTP design against each requirement the transport layer has to meet: reliability, congestion control, timing, addressing, staying up when a link fails, surviving an overload, and marking the messages. SCTP answers all of them, and using several addresses lets the link survive the loss of one of them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The SCTP transport mapping layer provides three security services to the protocol layer: a mechanism to authenticate control elements and forwarding elements at the transport level, so that unauthorized ones cannot take part in the control and data path processing of a ForCES network element; a mechanism to authenticate the protocol layer data and headers transferred between the two, so that incorrect data cannot be injected into protocol layer messages; and a mechanism to keep the confidentiality of that data and those headers, so that protocol layer information is not disclosed while it is transported.

Security choices are made by the operator and take effect during the pre-association phase of the ForCES protocol. An operator may use all, some or none of the security services in a control element to forwarding element connection, and may turn all the security functions off when operating in a secured environment or for other operational concerns, in some cases performance issues.

IPsec is used to provide the needed security mechanisms. IPsec is an IP-level security scheme transparent to higher-layer applications, so it can secure any transport layer protocol, which gives it the advantage that it can secure everything between the control element and the forwarding element without the transport mapping layer implementation having to know the details. Its architecture provides the message integrity and message confidentiality the transport layer requirements ask for, and mutual authentication and key exchange are provided by IKE.

A forwarding element or control element MUST support IKE with certificates for endpoint authentication, transport mode ESP, HMAC-SHA1-96 for message integrity protection, AES-CBC with 128-bit keys for message confidentiality, and replay protection. A compliant implementation SHOULD provide operational means for configuring the control element and forwarding element to negotiate other cipher suites and even to use manual keying.

To minimize operational configuration it is RECOMMENDED that only the IANA-issued SCTP protocol number, 132, be used as a selector in the Security Policy Database for ForCES, so that only a single SPD and SAD entry is needed. The setup MAY alternatively be extended to use the three SCTP TML port numbers as SPD selectors, which requires more SPD entries. In scenarios where multiple IP addresses are used within a single association and different policies are wanted per address, the document recommends following RFC 3554.
sections.plainLanguage: The transport can authenticate the peer, check that the messages were not altered and keep them private, all using IPsec underneath, so the transport layer itself does not have to know how. Certificates, transport mode ESP, HMAC-SHA1-96 and AES-CBC with 128-bit keys are the mandatory pieces.

items.title: Multi-homing
items.text: Several addresses for one peer, so a failure of one is invisible.

items.title: Runtime IP address binding
items.text: Addresses can be migrated to another node while running.

items.title: Reliability shades
items.text: Delivery can be reliable, partly reliable or unreliable.

items.title: Built-in heartbeats
items.text: Reachability faults are detected without another mechanism.

items.title: Multi-streaming
items.text: Many logical streams can share one association.

items.title: Message boundaries
items.text: Messages stay messages instead of becoming a byte stream.

items.title: Improved SYN DoS protection
items.text: The association setup is harder to flood.

items.title: Simplified replicasting
items.text: One message can be sent to several destinations.
